docs.title: NEMO Demonstrators
docs.text: Welcome to the documentation for NEMO Demonstrators.

docs.title: What is this?
docs.text: A collection of small, reproducible experiments run with the NEMO ocean model, each paired with the theory and the analysis code needed to understand the result.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• Run it yourself: help on how and where to run the simulations and their analysis.
  • Demonstrators: the notebooks and their NEMO configurations.
  • Methodology: notes and theoretical explanations on the notebooks.
  • Contributing: add your own demonstrator.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/justinebuisson606/NEMO_Demonstrators.git
cd NEMO_Demonstrators
python -m venv env_demo && source env_demo/bin/activate
pip install numpy matplotlib xarray netcdf4

docs.title: Build this site locally
docs.text:
pip install -r requirements-docs.txt
mkdocs serve

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
1. Fork the repository and create a branch.
  2. Add a notebook at the repository root (or in docs/extra/).
  3. Register it in the nav section of mkdocs.yml.
  4. Check locally with mkdocs serve, then open a pull request.

docs.title: Demonstrators
docs.text:
Each demonstrator is a notebook, with the NEMO configuration used to run it. The pages show saved outputs; to run the simulations, see Run it yourself. All configuration parameters are gathered in the configuration table.

Notebook NEMO configuration file Demonstrator 1 : Diffusive and dispersive properties of the tracer advection schemes The aim of this tutorial is to give the readers an opportunity to run the salt block simulation using the different advection schemes. Here we choose to use the transport of a block of salt to demonstrate how the diffusive and dispersive properties of the advection scheme impact the outcome of a simulation. demo1_cfg Demonstrator 2 : Qualitative comparison of performances based on spatial resolution The aim of this tutorial is to further dive into the dispersive and diffusive properties of the tracer advection schemes. Here we choose to transport sinusoidal signals at different frequencies to compare the performances of the different schemes based on the spatial resolution of the signal. demo2_cfg Demonstrator 3 : Diffusive and dispersive tracer advection schemes on eddies Here we choose to demonstrate how the diffusive and dispersive properties of the advection scheme impact the outcome of a simulation in the case of the formation of eddies. demo3_cfg Demonstrator 4 : Impact of explicit tracer diffusion schemes over a dispersive tracer advection scheme The aim of this tutorial is to dive into the interest of combining a diffusive operator with a dispersive scheme. FCT and UBS methods are examples of schemes where the numerical expression of the methods contains a dispersive term and a diffusive term. Here we choose to deliberately add a diffusive operator to a solely dispersive scheme (CEN) on the saltblock experience to attest of the benefits of having both properties. demo4_cfg Annex 1 - Saltblock moving diagonally This tutorial slightly complexifies the salt block simulation by changing from unidirectional advection to bi-directional advection and showcases the its consequences. annex1_cfg Annex 3 - CEN4 + BILAP = UBS The aim of this tutorial is to prove that the CEN4 combined with a Bi-Laplacian diffusion is equivalent to the UBS scheme. annex3_cfg

docs.title: Run the demonstrators yourself
docs.text: This website is static: GitHub Pages serves pre-rendered pages and cannot run code or launch NEMO. The notebooks shown under Demonstrators therefore display the outputs saved in the notebooks, and the buttons below take you to an environment where you can run them.

docs.title: What can run where
docs.text:
Part On this website Binder / Codespaces Your machine or HPC Reading notebooks, figures yes yes yes Analysis cells (plots from existing NetCDF output) no yes, if the output files are in the repository yes Launching NEMO simulations (.sh scripts) no no (NEMO must be compiled, MPI, input data) yes

Warning

The .sh scripts that start simulations need a working NEMO installation. They cannot run on GitHub Pages, in Binder, or in a standard Codespace.

docs.title: 1. Run locally (full workflow, including simulations)
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/justinebuisson606/NEMO_Demonstrators.git
cd NEMO_Demonstrators
# unzip the configuration for the demonstrator you want, e.g.
unzip demo1_cfg.zip
# then open the notebook, which calls the .sh scripts
jupyter lab "Demonstrator 1.ipynb"

Prerequisites: a compiled NEMO (see the NEMO documentation), Python with jupyterlab, numpy, matplotlib, xarray, netcdf4.

docs.title: 2. Analysis only, in the browser
docs.text: These open the repository in a Jupyter environment. For Binder to work, the repository needs an environment.yml or requirements.txt (a template is provided in binder/). Cells that call the simulation scripts will fail there.

docs.title: 3. Optional: ship the simulation output
docs.text: To make the analysis cells runnable online, commit the (small) NetCDF output files used by the figures, or host them (Zenodo, for example) and download them at the start of the notebook.

def phase_speed(f, dx, dt):
    """f[t, x] -> k, c(k) mesuré par la rotation de phase entre pas de temps."""
    F = np.fft.rfft(f - f.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True), axis=1)

    F=F[:,1:]

    A = np.abs(F[1:]/F[:-1])

Aim of Tutorial¶
docs.text: The aim of this tutorial is to further dive into the dispersive and diffusive properties of the tracer advection schemes. Here we choose to transport sinusoidal signals at different frequencies to compare the performances of the different schemes based on the spatial resolution of the signal.

Aim of Tutorial¶
docs.text:
The aim of this tutorial is to give the readers an opportunity to run the salt block simulation using the different advection schemes. Here we choose to use the transport of a block of salt to demonstrate how the diffusive and dispersive properties of the advection scheme impact the outcome of a simulation.

To run the simulations in this demonstrator you must have followed Tutorial 1 beforehand.

docs.title: Impact of explicit tracer diffusion schemes over a dispersive tracer advection scheme¶
Aim of Tutorial¶
docs.text: The aim of this tutorial is to dive into the interest of combining a diffusive operator with a dispersive scheme. FCT and UBS methods are examples of schemes where the numerical expression of the methods contains a dispersive term and a diffusive term. Here we choose to deliberately add a diffusive operator to a solely dispersive scheme (CEN) on the saltblock experience to attest of the benefits of having both properties.

The diffusive property of the UBS and FCT schemes, softens the swirls of the eddies. The eddy appears less structured and less detailed at small scales. Rather than keeping the abrupt differences between high values and low values (front) at small scale to form small detailed structures (filaments of salinity), the mixing tends to a global mean value of salinity and the destruction of detailed patterns.

def calculer_enstrophie(u, v, dx, dy):
    """
    Calcule l'enstrophie d'un champ de vitesse 2D.
    
    Paramètres:
    -----------
    u  : ndarray de taille (Ny, Nx)
         Composante de la vitesse selon l'axe X (horizontal).
    v  : ndarray de taille (Ny, Nx)

    enstrophie : float

    vorticity  : ndarray de taille (Ny, Nx)

    # 2. Calcul du tourbillon (vorticity) en 2D
    vorticity = np.nanmean(dv_dx - du_dy)
    
    
    return vorticity

docs.title: Phase speed and dampening effect : theory
Problem and strategy
docs.text:
We solve the 1D advection equation with a uniform velocity \(c_0 > 0\), in a periodic domain:

\[ \frac{\partial T}{\partial t} + c_0 \frac{\partial T}{\partial x} = 0 . \]

Why sinusoids? Any signal can be decomposed into a sum of sinusoids. If the scheme is linear and the current uniform, each Fourier mode evolves independently of the others. It is therefore enough to understand what the scheme does to one sinusoid; the signal is then the sum of all of them.

Exact solution. For \(T = e^{i(kx - \omega t)}\) the equation gives

\[ -i\omega + i c_0 k = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \omega = c_0 k , \]

so every wave travels at the same speed \(c_p = \omega/k = c_0\): there is no dispersion. A numerical scheme changes the relation \(\omega(k)\); this is what we compute below.

docs.title: CEN2 : Expression of the phase speed
docs.text:
The spatial discretisation of the transport equation is as follows :

\[ \partial_x T \approx \frac{T_{j+1} - T_{j-1}}{2\Delta x} = \frac{e^{i\theta} - e^{-i\theta }}{2\Delta x} T_j= \frac{2i \sin\theta}{2\Delta x} T_j \]

The time continuous part of the transport equation becomes :

\(\partial_t T = -i\omega T_j\)

Which gives us     \(c_p = \frac{\omega}{k} = c_0 \sin\theta/\theta\)

Small \(\theta\) expansion

\[ \frac{c_p}{c_0} = \frac{\sin\theta}{\theta} = 1 - \frac{\theta^2}{6} + \frac{\theta^4}{120} - \dots \]

Waves are always slower than \(c_0\), the more so the shorter they are. At \(\theta = \pi\), \(c_p = 0\): the \(2\Delta x\) wave does not move.

docs.title: CEN4 : Expression of the phase speed
docs.text:
The CEN4 scheme can be expressed as follows : $T_j^{cen4} = T_j^{cen2} - \frac{1}{6} \overline{ \delta_j \left[ \delta_{j+1/2}[T] \right]}^{j+1/2} $ with \(\overline{T}^{j+1/2} = (T_{j+1} + T_j)/2\) and \(\delta_j[T] = (T_{j+1} - T_j)\)

The spatial discretisation of the transport equation is as follows :

\[ \partial_x T \approx \frac{4}{3} \frac{T_{j+1} - T_{j-1}}{2\Delta x} - \frac{1}{6} \frac{T_{j+2} - T_{j-2}}{2\Delta x} = (\frac{4}{3}\frac{e^{i\theta} - e^{-i\theta }}{2\Delta x} -\frac{1}{6}\frac{e^{i2\theta} - e^{-i2\theta }}{\Delta x} ) T_j\ = (\frac{4}{3} \frac{i \sin\theta}{\Delta x} -\frac{1}{6}\frac{i \sin2\theta}{\Delta x}) T_j$ \]

The time continuous part of the transport equation becomes :

\(\partial_t T_j = -i\omega T_j\)

Which gives us \(c_p = \frac{\omega}{k} = c_0 (\frac{4}{3} \sin\theta/ - \frac{1}{6} \sin2\theta )/\theta\)

Small \(\theta\) expansion

Therefore \(c_p/c_0 \approx 1 - \theta^4/30\): the phase error is of order 4 instead of order 2 for CEN2.

docs.title: UBS : Expression of the phase speed
docs.text:
For \(c_0>0\), the discrete spatial derivative uses one point downstream and two upstream :

\[ \partial_t T_j \approx \frac{T_{j-2} - 6T_{j-1} + 3T_j + 2T_{j+1}}{6\Delta x}. \]

The time continuous part of the transport equation becomes :

\(\partial_t T = -i\omega T_j\),

Therefore, \(\omega = \omega_r + I\omega_i\) with

\(\omega_r = c_0 (\frac{4}{3} \sin\theta/ - \frac{1}{6} \sin2\theta )/\Delta x\)

Which gives us \(c_p = \frac{\omega_r}{k} = c_0 (\frac{4}{3} \sin\theta/ - \frac{1}{6} \sin2\theta )/\theta\)

And \(\omega_i = -\frac{c_0}{\Delta x}(1-\cos\theta)^2/3\)

Interpretation. The wave is \(e^{\omega_i t}e^{i(kx - \omega_r t)}\):

  • the real part \(\omega_r\) is the same as CEN4, so UBS has the same \(c_p\) as CEN4;
  • the imaginary part \(\omega_i = -c_0 D/\Delta x < 0\) is a damping that kills short waves while leaving long waves almost untouched. For small \(\theta\), \(D \approx \theta^4/12\); at \(\theta=\pi/2\), \(D = 1/3\); at \(\theta = \pi\), \(D = 4/3\). UBS is CEN4 plus a fourth-order (bi-Laplacian-like) diffusion.

docs.title: Time stepping
docs.text:
For \(C \ll 1\) the time error is far smaller than the spatial error (\(\propto\theta^2\) or \(\theta^4\)). The time scheme matters when \(C\) approaches 1.

\(C = c_0\Delta t/\Delta x\)

For the simulations in the demonstrator :

docs.title: Measuring the phase speed from model output
docs.text:
For a linear scheme on a periodic domain, take the spatial Fourier transform of the field at each output time:

\[ F_m(t) = \sum_{j} T_j(t)\, e^{-i k_m x_j}, \qquad k_m = \frac{2\pi m}{N\Delta x}, \quad \theta_m = \frac{2\pi m}{N}. \]

(With numpy.fft.rfft the kernel is \(e^{-ikx}\), so a wave \(e^{i(kx-\omega t)}\) gives a coefficient \(\propto e^{-i\omega t}\).) Each mode is multiplied by the same complex factor between two outputs separated by \(\Delta t_{out}\):

\[ R_m = \frac{F_m(t + \Delta t_{out})}{F_m(t)} = e^{-i\omega\Delta t_{out}} \;\Longrightarrow\; \omega_r = -\frac{\arg R_m}{\Delta t_{out}}, \quad \omega_i = \frac{\ln|R_m|}{\Delta t_{out}}, \quad c_p = \frac{\omega_r}{k_m}. \]

Averaging \(R_m\) over all pairs of consecutive outputs, weighted by the amplitude \(|F_m(t)F_m(t+\Delta t_{out})|\), reduces the noise (modes with almost zero amplitude, such as the spectral zeros of a square block, have an unreliable phase).

Warning "Phase aliasing" : \(\arg R_m\) is only defined modulo \(2\pi\). The measurement is valid if the phase rotation between two outputs is below \(\pi\):

\[ k c_0 \Delta t_{out} < \pi \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \theta < \pi\Delta x/(c_0\Delta t_{out}) \]

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: In simulations, time and space are divided into discrete grids and the continuous differential equations of motion (such as the Navier–Stokes equation) are discretized into finite-difference equations, these discrete equations are in general unidentical to the original differential equations, so the simulated system behaves differently than the intended physical system.

docs.title: Study of a first order diffusive scheme (UP1):
docs.text:
Consider the 1D linear advection equation with constant velocity \(c\):

\[ \frac{\partial T}{\partial t}+c\frac{\partial T}{\partial x}=0 \]

The spatial discretisation of the transport equation is as follows :

\[ \partial_x T_j \approx \frac{T_{j} - T_{j-1}}{\Delta x} \]

Using a Taylor series expansion to evaluate the truncation error :

\[ \frac{T_{j} - T_{j-1}}{2\Delta x} = \partial_x T + \frac {\Delta x }{2} \partial_x^2 T + \mathcal{O}(\Delta x ^2) \]

Substituting this back into the governing equation reveals the modified equation:

\[ \frac{\partial T}{\partial t}+c\frac{\partial T}{\partial x}= - c \frac {\Delta x }{2} \partial_x^2 T + \mathcal{O}(\Delta x ^2) \]

The presence of the 2nd-order spatial derivative \(\frac{\partial ^{2}T}{\partial x^{2}}\) mathematically dictates that the scheme is purely diffusive.

docs.title: Physical consequences of diffusion
docs.text:
The consequence of the dispersion is that even-order derivative errors act like numerical viscosity. The viscosity dampens the signal, smoothes out the edges. When resolving sharp profiles (like a step function or square pulse) a diffusive model will reduce the high magnitude gradients, turning a steep slop into a gentle slope, a step into a hill.

Intricate structures like eddies will become less structured at small scales.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
In simulations, time and space are divided into discrete grids and the continuous differential equations of motion (such as the Navier–Stokes equation) are discretized into finite-difference equations, these discrete equations are in general unidentical to the original differential equations, so the simulated system behaves differently than the intended physical system.

An example of a dispersive scheme in NEMO 5.0 is the CENtred advection scheme (CEN).

docs.title: Study of a second order dispersive scheme (CEN2):
docs.text:
Consider the 1D linear advection equation with constant velocity \(c\):

\[ \frac{\partial T}{\partial t}+c\frac{\partial T}{\partial x}=0 \]

The spatial discretisation of the transport equation is as follows :

\[ \partial_x T_j \approx \frac{T_{j+1} - T_{j-1}}{2\Delta x} \]

Using a Taylor series expansion to evaluate the truncation error :

\[ \frac{T_{j+1} - T_{j-1}}{2\Delta x} = \partial_x T + \frac {\Delta x ^2}{6} \partial_x^3 T + \mathcal{O}(\Delta x ^4) \]

Substituting this back into the governing equation reveals the modified equation:

\[ \frac{\partial T}{\partial t}+c\frac{\partial T}{\partial x}= - c \frac {\Delta x ^2}{6} \partial_x^3 T + \mathcal{O}(\Delta x ^4) \]

The presence of the 3rd-order spatial derivative \(\frac{\partial ^{3}T}{\partial x^{3}}\) mathematically dictates that the scheme is purely dispersive rather than dissipative.

docs.title: Physical consequences of dispersion
docs.text:
The consequence of the dispersion is that every numerical wave component travels slower than the true physical speed c. When resolving sharp profiles (like a step function or square pulse) containing high frequencies, these high-frequency components lag severely behind the main wave packet. This results in unphysical oscillations trailing behind the wavefront. Overall the signal loses its shape.

These wiggles are called side lobes and result in tracer values out of the authorised bounds of the initial distribution of the tracer. This can be quite problematic because it can generate unphysical values of the tracers (eg. negative salinity).
